transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Well, I guess what brings me in is... I just feel like I’m constantly running on a motor lately. Like, I finish one thing at school or at home and I just immediately jump right into the next thing without a break. 

Speaking of school, I teach special education, and they just rolled out this completely new software system for the kids' files. It's supposed to be this fancy cloud-based thing, but the interface is just a total disaster. I was talking to Linda down in the resource room about it on Tuesday—or no, wait, it was Wednesday because they were serving that weird meatloaf in the cafeteria—and she couldn't get it to save her notes either. We spent like an hour trying to call IT, and you know how the district IT guys are, they never pick up the phone before noon. 

But anyway, what was I... right, yeah, I just never seem to be able to shut myself off. I just keep going and going.
Along with feeling like you're constantly on the go, have you also noticed a change in your mood—like feeling unusually happy, elated, or more irritable than usual?

Unusually happy? No, I wouldn't say that. My mood is pretty much the same as always. I'm not euphoric or anything. Though, I will admit I was pretty thrilled on Monday when they finally fixed the copy machine in the teacher's lounge. It had been jamming for three weeks straight, and every time you tried to print double-sided, it just completely shredded the paper. 

Jerry—he teaches history—he actually tried to fix it himself with a paperclip, which was hilarious but totally made it worse. He's always doing stuff like that. Last year he tried to fix the microwave and we couldn't heat up our lunches for a month. I ended up eating so many cold sandwiches because of him. I actually found this great deli down the street because of that, though. They make a fantastic pastrami on rye with that really spicy mustard. Have you been there? The one over on 5th? They wrap it in that thick butcher paper, it's really old school. 

But, uh... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, my mood. Yeah, no, I don't feel irritable or elated or anything like that. Just... you know, just can't seem to stop moving.
Can you tell me if you've felt this way—constantly on the go and unable to slow down—for as long as you can remember, even back in childhood, or is this a new change from how you used to be?

Well, no, it's definitely not new. It's been like this... gosh, pretty much forever. My mother actually used to joke that even back in elementary school, I basically taught the class from my seat. I was always out of my chair, or I'd be talking, or I'd just blurting things out before the teacher even finished giving directions. 

Mrs. Gable, my third-grade teacher—she was this tiny woman who always wore these enormous, colorful scarves. Like, they were bigger than she was! She had this one scarf with little owls on it that I always stared at. Anyway, she tried to get me to stay in my seat by putting masking tape on the floor around my desk. It was supposed to be my "zone." But then the janitor got mad because the tape left sticky residue on the linoleum, and you know how hard it is to get that stuff off once it sets in. We use this citrus solvent at the school now that smells amazing, like fresh oranges, but back then they just used these awful chemical cleaners that gave everyone a headache. 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the family change... or no, childhood. Yeah, this is just who I am. It's been part of me long before adulthood, not something that just started up recently. It's just... always been this way.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a lifelong (since elementary school), pervasive pattern of hyperactivity ('constantly on the go,' unable to slow down), impulsivity (blurting out answers, leaving seat), and marked distractibility/tangentiality (repeated derailment into unrelated tangents about coworkers, food, cleaning solvents).
